claim: Frischella perrara is a proteobacterium that is a widely distributed gut symbiont of honey bees.
source: The proteobacterium Frischella perrara is a widely distributed gut symbiont of honey bees.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: F. perrara colonizes a specific niche in the hindgut of honey bees.
source: It colonizes a specific niche in the hindgut and causes a characteristic melanization response.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: F. perrara causes a characteristic melanization response in honey bees.
source: It colonizes a specific niche in the hindgut and causes a characteristic melanization response.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Three point mutations in genes encoding integration host factor (IHF) were independently isolated in F. perrara.
source: Here, we independently isolated three point mutations in genes encoding the DNA-binding protein integration host factor (IHF) in F. perrara.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by genome sequencing data presented in the results.

claim: IHF mutants abolished the production of an aryl polyene metabolite causing the yellow colony morphotype of F. perrara.
source: These mutants abolished the production of an aryl polyene metabolite causing the yellow colony morphotype of F. perrara.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by HPLC-MS data in Figure 2.

claim: Inoculation of microbiota-free bees with one of the IHF mutants drastically decreased gut colonization of F. perrara.
source: Inoculation of microbiota-free bees with one of the mutants drastically decreased gut colonization of F. perrara.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by CFU data in Figure 3.

claim: IHF affects the expression of potential colonization factors including genes for adhesion (type 4 pili), interbacterial competition (type 6 secretion systems), and secondary metabolite production (colibactin and aryl polyene biosynthesis).
source: Using RNAseq, we found that IHF affects the expression of potential colonization factors, including genes for adhesion (type 4 pili), interbacterial competition (type 6 secretion systems), and secondary metabolite production (colibactin and aryl polyene biosynthesis).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNAseq data in Figure 4.

claim: Gene deletions of IHF-regulated components revealed different colonization defects depending on the presence of other bee gut bacteria.
source: Gene deletions of these components revealed different colonization defects depending on the presence of other bee gut bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by colonization data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: One of the T6SS mutants did not induce the scab phenotype despite colonizing at high levels.
source: Interestingly, one of the T6SS mutants did not induce the scab phenotype anymore despite colonizing at high levels, suggesting an unexpected role in bacteria-host interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: IHF is conserved across many bacteria.
source: IHF is conserved across many bacteria and may also regulate host colonization in other animal symbionts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is based on established knowledge about IHF.

claim: IHF may regulate host colonization in other animal symbionts.
source: IHF is conserved across many bacteria and may also regulate host colonization in other animal symbionts.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings in F. perrara.

claim: The Western honey bee, Apis mellifera, harbors relatively simple yet highly specialized gut microbiota composed of 8–10 bacterial genera.
source: Honey bees harbor relatively simple yet highly specialized gut microbiota composed of 8–10 bacterial genera (Kwong and Moran, 2016; Bonilla-Rosso and Engel, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The wide distribution of bee gut microbiota communities across social bees suggests long evolutionary associations with the host.
source: The wide distribution of these communities across social bees suggests long evolutionary associations with the host (Kwong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Different members of the bee microbiota colonize distinct physical niches along the gut.
source: Moreover, different members of the bee microbiota colonize distinct physical niches along the gut. Lactobacilli and Bifidobacteria predominate in the posterior hindgut (rectum), while Gammaproteobacteria (Frischella perrara and Gilliamella species) and a Betaproteobacterium (Snodgrassella alvi) preferentially colonize the anterior hindgut (ileum and adjacent pylorus, i.e., the transition zone between midgut and ileum) (Kwong and Moran, 2016; Engel et al., 2015a; Martinson et al., 2011; Powell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: F. perrara preferentially colonizes the transition zone between the midgut and the ileum, that is, the pylorus.
source: F. perrara preferentially colonizes the transition zone between the midgut and the ileum, that is, the pylorus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Colonization with F. perrara leads to the appearance of a brown to black material on the luminal side of the epithelial surface between the cuticle layer of the host tissue and the adherent F. perrara cells.
source: Moreover, colonization with F. perrara leads to the appearance of a brown to black material on the luminal side of the epithelial surface between the cuticle layer of the host tissue and the adherent F. perrara cells (Engel et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The scab phenotype forms after 5–7 d post-colonization.
source: This so-called scab phenotype forms after 5–7 d post-colonization and has so far not been reported to be triggered by any other gut symbiont than F. perrara.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: F. perrara elicits a specific immune response that includes the upregulation of the host melanization pathway likely responsible for the formation of the scab phenotype.
source: Transcriptome analysis of the host showed that F. perrara elicits a specific immune response that includes the upregulation of the host melanization pathway likely responsible for the formation of the scab phenotype (Emery et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: F. perrara is highly prevalent across worker bees and colonies of A. mellifera.
source: F. perrara is highly prevalent across worker bees and colonies of A. mellifera (Engel et al., 2015a; Kešnerová et al., 2020), and related bacteria have also been found in Apis cerana (Wolter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Between 25 and 80% of all worker bees of a colony harbor a visible scab phenotype in the pylorus region of the gut.
source: Moreover, between 25 and 80% of all worker bees of a colony harbor a visible scab phenotype in the pylorus region of the gut, which has been shown to strongly correlate with a high abundance of F. perrara (Engel et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The genome of F. perrara contains several genomic islands that may be involved in the specific interaction with the host.
source: Genome sequencing of the type strain of F. perrara and comparison with other genomes of the Orbaceae family revealed the presence of several genomic islands that may be involved in the specific interaction of F. perrara with the host (Engel et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: F. perrara genomic islands include a biosynthetic gene cluster for the production of the genotoxic metabolite colibactin (Clb), two distinct type VI secretion systems (T6SSs) and associated effector proteins, type I secretion systems, and fimbrial low-molecular-weight protein (Flp) pili genes.
source: These include a biosynthetic gene cluster for the production of the genotoxic metabolite colibactin (Clb), two distinct type VI secretion systems (T6SSs) and associated effector proteins, type I secretion systems, and fimbrial low-molecular-weight protein (Flp) pili genes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Culturing F. perrara type strain PEB0191 on modified tryptone yeast glucose (mTYG) agar resulted in the formation of yellow colonies.
source: Culturing F. perrara type strain PEB0191 (Engel et al., 2013) on modified tryptone yeast glucose (mTYG) agar resulted in the formation of yellow colonies.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: White colonies of F. perrara occasionally appeared among the yellow ones.
source: However, we occasionally observed the appearance of larger white colonies among the yellow ones (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Three stable 'white' variants of F. perrara PEB0191 were isolated.
source: However, three white colonies that we identified in independent experiments did not change their appearance anymore, suggesting that we had isolated stable 'white' variants of F. perrara PEB0191 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genome sequencing of the white variants revealed the presence of three different non-synonymous point mutations in the genes encoding the IHF.
source: Genome sequencing of the white variants revealed the presence of three different non-synonymous point mutations in the genes encoding the IHF.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by genome sequencing data.

claim: IHF is a widely distributed DNA-binding protein consisting of the IhfA/B heterocomplex.
source: IHF is a widely distributed DNA-binding protein consisting of the IhfA/B heterocomplex (Friedman, 1988; Freundlich et al., 1992; Goosen and van de Putte, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two point mutations in IHF were identical to each other, but occurred in the different subunits of IHF (ihfA and ihfB), resulting in a proline to lysine change at amino acid positions 82 and 83, respectively.
source: Strikingly, two point mutations were identical to each other, but occurred in the different subunits of IHF (ihfA and ihfB), resulting in a proline to lysine change at amino acid positions 82 and 83, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The third point mutation resulted in a lysine to serine change at position 38 of IhfA.
source: The third point mutation resulted in a lysine to serine change at position 38 of IhfA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Homology modeling showed that the mutated amino acids are located in the region interacting with DNA, suggesting that the three mutations impact the DNA-binding properties of IHF.
source: Homology modeling showed that these amino acids are located in the region interacting with DNA, suggesting that the three mutations impact the DNA-binding properties of IHF (Figure 1D; Rice et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the results, shown in Figure 1D, and supported by a citation.

claim: The ihfA* strain consistently formed larger colonies than the wt strain on mTYG agar.
source: While the ihfA* strain consistently formed larger colonies than the wt strain on mTYG agar (Figure 1A and B), there was no significant difference in growth in liquid culture (permutation test, p=0.097; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A, 1B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was no significant difference in growth between ihfA* and wt in liquid culture.
source: While the ihfA* strain consistently formed larger colonies than the wt strain on mTYG agar (Figure 1A and B), there was no significant difference in growth in liquid culture (permutation test, p=0.097; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: Cells of the ihfA* mutant strain were on average slightly longer than cells of the wt.
source: However, light microscopy showed that cells of the mutant strain were on average slightly longer than cells of the wt (Kolgomorov–Smirnov test p<0.0001, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C with statistical analysis.

claim: F. perrara PEB0191 encodes a genomic island that is homologous to aryl polyene (APE) biosynthetic gene clusters present in other Gammaproteobacteria.
source: F. perrara PEB0191 encodes a genomic island that is homologous to aryl polyene (APE) biosynthetic gene clusters present in other Gammaproteobacteria (Figure 2A; Cimermancic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results, shown in Figure 2A, and supported by a citation.

claim: APEs are polyunsaturated carboxylic acids conferring a yellow pigmentation to bacterial cells.
source: APEs are polyunsaturated carboxylic acids conferring a yellow pigmentation to bacterial cells (Goel et al., 2002; Poplawsky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HPLC-HES-HRMS analysis revealed a strongly UV-Vis-absorbent ion peak at m/z 323.1647 [M+H]+ in F. perrara wt cell extracts.
source: The data revealed a strongly UV-Vis-absorbent ion peak at m/z 323.1647 [M+H]+, which had a suggested molecular formula of C21H23O3 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: In the ihfA* mutant, the ion at m/z 323.1647 was only present at trace amounts.
source: In the ihfA* mutant, this ion was only present at trace amounts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MS-MS fragmentation experiments, UV-Vis spectrum, and NMR data suggest an aryl polyene structure identical to that reported in Cimermancic et al., 2014; Schöner et al., 2016.
source: The characteristic ions detected in MS-MS fragmentation experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the UV-Vis spectrum with an absorption maximum at 415 nm (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) in conjunction with NMR data (Figure 2—figure supplements 3–10), suggest an aryl polyene structure identical to that reported in Cimermancic et al., 2014; Schöner et al., 2016; Figure 2D.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in multiple figure supplements and citations.

claim: Comparison of the organic extracts of F. perrara wt and Escherichia coli CFT073 provided further evidence that both produce the same compound.
source: Comparison of the organic extracts of F. perrara wt and Escherichia coli CFT073 provided further evidence that both produce the same compound (Figure 2—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 11.

claim: The APE pathway is responsible for the yellow color of the wt colonies of F. perrara and is suppressed in the ihfA* mutant.
source: Combined, these results suggest that the APE pathway is responsible for the yellow color of the wt colonies of F. perrara and is suppressed in the ihfA* mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Colonization with F. perrara wt resulted in a visible scab in 50 and 80% of all bees after 5 and 10 d of colonization, respectively.
source: Colonization with the wt strain resulted in a visible scab in 50 and 80% of all bees after 5 and 10 d of colonization, respectively (n = 18 and n = 36 for both treatments for day 5 and day 10, respectively, Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: None of the bees colonized with the ihfA* mutant developed a visible scab phenotype.
source: In contrast, none of the bees colonized with the ihfA* mutant developed a visible scab phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: At day 10 post-colonization, bees colonized with the wt strain showed significantly higher CFUs than the ihfA* mutant.
source: However, at day 10 post-colonization, bees colonized with the wt strain showed significantly higher CFUs than the ihfA* mutant (Figure 3C, Wilcoxon rank-sum test p-value<0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: In 50% of all bees at day 10 post-colonization, the colonization levels of ihfA* were below the detection limit of 500 CFUs.
source: In fact, in 50% of all bees (n = 36) the colonization levels of ihfA* were below the detection limit of 500 CFUs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At day 10 post colonization, there was a significant difference in the colonization levels of the wt and ihfA* in both the pylorus and the ileum.
source: The results were comparable to those obtained for the whole gut: at day 10 post colonization, there was a significant difference in the colonization levels of the wt and ihfA* in both the pylorus and the ileum (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p-value<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: Between day 4 and day 8 post inoculation, the abundance of the wt increased rapidly to about 10^6 CFUs per gut and then steadily further to 10^7 CFUs per gut until the last time point.
source: Between day 4 and day 8 post inoculation, the abundance of the wt increased rapidly to about 106 CFUs per gut and then steadily further to 107 CFUs per gut until the last time point.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The levels of the ihfA* mutant remained low until day 10 post colonization and reached on average no more than 10^5 CFUs per gut until the last time point at day 22 post colonization.
source: In contrast, the levels of the ihfA* mutant remained low until day 10 post colonization and reached on average no more than 105 CFUs per gut until the last time point at day 22 post colonization.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ihfA* has a strong colonization defect with delayed colonization dynamics compared to the wt, does not reach the same bacterial loads, and does not cause the scab phenotype.
source: In summary, these results show that ihfA* has a strong colonization defect. It has a delayed colonization dynamics compared to the wt, does not reach the same bacterial loads, and does not cause the scab phenotype, even though the bees were inoculated with more viable cells of ihfA* than the wt.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: 358 out of 2337 genes encoded in the genome of F. perrara were differentially expressed with a log2-fold change >|2| between the wt and ihfA* strains.
source: We found that 358 out of 2337 genes encoded in the genome of F. perrara were differentially expressed with a log2-fold change >|2| between the two strains (Fisher's exact test with p<0.05 and false discovery rate (FDR) <5%).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNAseq data.

claim: 237 and 121 genes were up- and downregulated in F. perrara wt versus ihfA*, respectively.
source: Of those, 237 and 121 genes were up- and downregulated in F. perrara wt versus ihfA*, respectively (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Among the genes upregulated in the wt, 'Intracellular trafficking, secretion, and vesicular transport' (COG U), 'Extracellular structure' (COG W), 'Lipid transport and metabolism' (COG I), 'Mobilome: prophages and transposases' (COG X), and 'Secondary metabolites biosynthesis, transport and catabolism' (COG Q) were significantly enriched.
source: Among the genes upregulated in the wt, 'Intracellular trafficking, secretion, and vesicular transport' (COG U), 'Extracellular structure' (COG W), 'Lipid transport and metabolism' (COG I), 'Mobilome: prophages and transposases' (COG X), and 'Secondary metabolites biosynthesis, transport and catabolism' (COG Q) were significantly enriched (Fisher's exact test, BH-adjusted p-value<0.01; see Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Genes belonging to enriched COG categories include different subunits and effectors of the two T6SSs of F. perrara, the Clb biosynthesis gene cluster, various components of the Flp pili, and an RTX (repeats in toxin) toxin belonging to the type I secretion system family.
source: Genes belonging to these three categories include different subunits and effectors of the two T6SSs of F. perrara, the Clb biosynthesis gene cluster, various components of the Flp pili, and an RTX (repeats in toxin) toxin belonging to the type I secretion system family (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: The genes of the APE biosynthesis gene cluster were among the upregulated genes in wt versus ihfA*.
source: Also, the genes of the APE biosynthesis gene cluster were among the upregulated genes, which is in line with the production of the corresponding metabolites in the wt but not in the mutant strain (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and consistent with data in Figure 2.

claim: T6SS and Clb biosynthesis genes were among the genes with the highest fold changes relative to ihfA* mutant.
source: T6SS and Clb biosynthesis genes were among the genes with the highest fold changes relative to ihfA* mutant (Figure 4B, 28 of 32 genes with log2-fold change > 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 64% of the upregulated genes (152/237) belonged to the F. perrara-specific gene content.
source: Moreover, 64% of the upregulated genes (152/237) belonged to the F. perrara-specific gene content as based on our previously published genome comparison of F. perrara PEB0191 with four other strains of the family Orbaceae (three of the genus Gilliamella and one of the genus Orbus, Figure 4—source data 1; Engel et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation.

claim: Among the 121 downregulated genes, only COG category O ('Posttranslational modification, protein turnover, chaperones') was statistically enriched.
source: Among the 121 downregulated genes, only COG category O ('Posttranslational modification, protein turnover, chaperones') was statistically enriched (Fisher's exact test, BH-adjusted p-value<0.01, see Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A total of 260 (149 up and 111 down) and 298 (162 up and 136 down) genes were differentially expressed at day 5 and day 10 post colonization relative to growth in vitro.
source: A total of 260 (149 up and 111 down) and 298 (162 up and 136 down) genes were differentially expressed at day 5 and day 10 post colonization relative to growth in vitro (log2-fold change >|2|, quasi-likelihood F-test with p<0.05 and FDR < 5%, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNAseq data.

claim: At both time points (day 5 and day 10), the COG category 'Carbohydrate transport and metabolism' (COG G) was significantly enriched among the genes upregulated in vivo relative to the entire genome.
source: At both time points, the COG category 'Carbohydrate transport and metabolism' (COG G) was significantly enriched among the genes upregulated in vivo relative to the entire genome (Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: At time point day 10, the COG category (P) 'Inorganic ion transport and metabolism' was also enriched.
source: In addition, at time point day 10, also the COG category (P) 'Inorganic ion transport and metabolism' was enriched (P adj<0.01, Fisher's exact test, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Most of the T6SS machinery, APE biosynthesis, pilus, and iron uptake genes were expressed at both time points in vivo, and to similar levels as in vitro.
source: Indeed, when comparing count-normalized gene expression (as measured by transcripts per million [TPM]) across the different conditions, we found that most of the T6SS machinery, APE biosynthesis, pilus, and iron uptake genes were expressed at both time points in vivo, and to similar levels as in vitro (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Clb genomic island and some of the VgrG-like T6SS effector genes had clearly lower TPM values in vivo than in vitro, yet higher than in ihfA* in vitro.
source: Only the Clb genomic island and some of the VgrG-like T6SS effector genes had clearly lower TPM values in vivo than in vitro, yet higher than in ihfA* in vitro (Figure 5C and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C and F.

claim: Six different non-polar in-frame gene-deletion mutants of potential colonization factors regulated by IHF were created.
source: This allowed us to create six different non-polar in-frame gene-deletion mutants of potential colonization factors regulated by IHF (Key Resources Table).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: The ΔapeA-R mutant was the only strain not forming yellow colonies anymore.
source: The ΔapeA-R mutant was the only strain not forming yellow colonies anymore (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with the idea that the aryl polyene pathway is responsible for the yellow color.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the Δhcp1/Δhcp2 and ΔpilE strains had lower CFU counts than the wt strain when OD600 was corresponded to CFU counts.
source: Moreover, we corresponded OD600 to CFU counts and found that both the Δhcp1/Δhcp2 and ΔpilE strains had lower counts than the wt strain (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The wt successfully colonized the pylorus/ileum region of all analyzed gnotobiotic bees (median = 9.56 * 10^6 ± 5.06 * 10^6 CFUs per gut; n = 18 bees, two independent experiments) and induced the scab phenotype in 16 of 18 bees.
source: As expected, the wt successfully colonized the pylorus/ileum region of all analyzed gnotobiotic bees (median = 9.56 * 106 ± 5.06 * 106 CFUs per gut; n = 18 bees, two independent experiments) and induced the scab phenotype in 16 of 18 bees (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: The ihfA* colonized poorly compared to the wt (median = 1.46 * 10^4 ± 3.19 * 10^5 CFUs per gut, n = 20 bees, Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.001), and not a single bee developed the scab phenotype.
source: In contrast, the ihfA* colonized poorly compared to the wt (median = 1.46 * 104 ± 3.19 * 105 CFUs per gut, n = 20 bees, Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.001), and not a single bee developed the scab phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis.

claim: Of the six tested gene-deletion mutants, only the mutant of T6SS-1 (Δhcp1) reached wt colonization levels and also induced the scab phenotype in most of the bees (15 out of 20).
source: Of the six tested gene-deletion mutants, only the mutant of T6SS-1 (Δhcp1) reached wt colonization levels and also induced the scab phenotype in most of the bees (15 out of 20).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Clb biosynthesis gene cluster mutant ΔclbB induced the scab phenotype in all but one bee, despite the fact that the colonization levels were about twofold lower than for the wt.
source: For example, the Clb biosynthesis gene cluster mutant ΔclbB induced the scab phenotype in all but one bee, despite the fact that the colonization levels were about twofold lower than for the wt (median = 4.24 * 106 ± 2.87 * 106 CFUs per gut).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The gene-deletion mutant of the T6SS-2 (Δhcp2) and the double mutant of both T6SSs (Δhcp1/Δhcp2) reached similar colonization levels as the ΔclbB mutant, yet none of the bees colonized with these two mutants developed the scab phenotype.
source: The gene-deletion mutant of the T6SS-2 (Δhcp2) and the double mutant of both T6SSs (Δhcp1/Δhcp2) reached similar colonization levels as the ΔclbB mutant. Yet, none of the bees colonized with these two mutants developed the scab phenotype not even those that had very high bacterial counts (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The deletion mutant of the APE biosynthesis pathway (ΔapeA-R) showed variable colonization: for some bees no colonization was detected, while others showed similar colonization levels as the wt of F. perrara.
source: The deletion mutant of the APE biosynthesis pathway (ΔapeA-R) showed again a different colonization phenotype: for some bees no colonization was detected, while others showed similar colonization levels as the wt of F. perrara.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The ΔapeA-R mutant still induced the scab phenotype, but only in the bees that had high bacterial loads.
source: However, in contrast to the Δhcp2 and the Δhcp1/Δhcp2 mutants, the ΔapeA-R mutant still induced the scab phenotype, but only in the bees that had high bacterial loads.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The ΔpilE mutant had the strongest impact on colonization: only 5 out of 20 bees had detectable levels of F. perrara in the gut and none of the bees developed the scab phenotype.
source: Finally, the ΔpilE mutant had the strongest impact on colonization. Only 5 out of 20 bees had detectable levels of F. perrara in the gut (limit of detection: 75 CFUs per gut) and none of the bees developed the scab phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Electron microscopy imaging revealed the ΔpilE strain did not have pili.
source: Electron microscopy imaging revealed this strain did not have pili, confirming the ΔpilE mutation affects the formation of these structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: F. perrara wt was found to colonize the pylorus region, forming a dense biofilm in close proximity to the host and occupying the crypts.
source: As previously reported Engel et al., 2015a, F. perrara wt was found to colonize the pylorus region, forming a dense biofilm in close proximity to the host and occupying the crypts.
evidence: This is stated in the results, shown in Figure 6B, and supported by a citation.

claim: A similar colonization pattern to wt was observed for Δhcp1, Δhcp2, Δhcp1/Δhcp2, ΔclbB, and ΔapeA-R.
source: A similar colonization pattern was observed for Δhcp1, Δhcp2, Δhcp1/Δhcp2, ΔclbB, and ΔapeA-R.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: For the ihfA* and ΔpilE mutants, no bacteria were identified in the analyzed gut sections.
source: In contrast, for the ihfA* and ΔpilE mutants, we did not identify any bacteria in the analyzed gut sections, which is in agreement with the low colonization levels of these mutants detected by CFU plating.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Dark spots corresponding to scab material were found along the cuticular lining colonized by bacteria for the ΔclbB, Δhcp1, and ΔapeA-R, but not for the Δhcp2 and Δhcp1/Δhcp2 mutants.
source: Dark spots corresponding to scab material were found along the cuticular lining colonized by bacteria for the ΔclbB, Δhcp1, and ΔapeA-R, but not for the Δhcp2 and Δhcp1/Δhcp2 mutants, which matches the visual inspections of the dissected guts for the presence/absence of the scab phenotype across the different strains (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The inability of the Δhcp2 and Δhcp1/Δhcp2 mutants to trigger the scab phenotype cannot be explained by an altered localization in the gut.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that the inability of the Δhcp2 and Δhcp1/Δhcp2 mutants to trigger the scab phenotype cannot be explained by an altered localization in the gut.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FISH microscopy data in Figure 6B.
